data.content_ref: inline:The target asserts that when the divergence stratum is empty (checklist and expert always agree), no single-evaluation evidence can distinguish genuine gain from mere compliance. But the problem asks to argue for or against the claim that a panel following a checklist will produce more reliable judgments than a single expert, and to identify what evidence within a single evaluation distinguishes genuine reliability gain from checklist compliance that happens to track the right answer. Even under full agreement, a corrupted-checklist control run within the same evaluation creates synthetic divergence: if the original-checklist panel reliably beats the corrupted-checklist panel, that single-evaluation contrast isolates the checklist's causal contribution to correctness. The target's countercondition explicitly admits this possibility ('A corrupted-checklist control reveals a contrast even with an empty divergence stratum'), yet the main claim still declares the problem unsatisfiable. The counterexample invalidates the target's core conclusion because a single evaluation can include a control arm that distinguishes genuine gain from compliance even when the original panel and expert never disagree.
